docs.title: steercert
docs.text:
Does the direction your safety monitor reads also control the behaviour?

Linear probes on activations are now used as low-cost safety monitors, and activation steering is used to change model behaviour at inference time. Both work with a direction in a model's residual stream, and it is common to assume that a direction that detects a behaviour can also change it, or that a monitor reading one direction sees every way the behaviour can be moved.

steercert tests that assumption. Given per-example gradients of a behavioural functional at an intervention site, it builds the effect Gramian \(W = \mathbb{E}[g g^\top]\) and reports, for any direction:

Question Quantity How much of the achievable steering effect does this direction capture? RMS write efficiency \(\sqrt{w^\top W w / \lambda_{\max}(W)}\) How much leverage is there at this site at all? absolute leverage \(\lVert \bar g \rVert\) What is the strongest direction a probe cannot see? dark direction, and its efficiency Does the direction beat construction-matched controls? control families with degeneracy checks Does the certificate predict real interventions here? held-out Spearman ranking

The certificate needs one backward pass per batch and no interventions. Finite interventions are used only to validate it.

import steercert
from steercert.synthetic import decoupled_site

site = decoupled_site(overlap=0.1)
report = steercert.audit(site.gradients, probe=site.read_direction,
                         states=site.states, labels=site.labels)
print(report.summary())

Scope

The bundled behavioural functionals are next-token proxies. A certificate is a cheap, local, first-order screen. Validate conclusions about deployed behaviour with generation-level evaluation.

docs.title: CI regression checks
docs.text:
A steering vector or a probe-based monitor validated on one checkpoint can stop working after a fine-tune, a quantisation or a model update. A saved audit report turns that into a test.

steercert demo --out report.json        # synthetic example report
steercert summary report.json           # print a saved report
steercert check report.json \
    --min-efficiency deployed_vector=0.5 \
    --min-ranking 0.7 \
    --min-leverage 0.1

check exits with status 1 and prints one FAIL line per violated threshold.

Option Fails when --min-efficiency NAME=V a direction's RMS efficiency is below V --max-efficiency NAME=V a direction's RMS efficiency is above V (for example a monitor that must stay blind to a channel) --min-ranking V the certificate-to-measurement Spearman is below V or missing --min-leverage V absolute leverage \(\lVert\bar g\rVert\) is below V --min-stable-rank V stable rank is below V --fail-on-warnings any warning finding is present

The same checks are available in Python as report.check(...) and steercert.check_report(dict, ...).

docs.title: GitHub Actions sketch
docs.text:
- run: python scripts/audit_release_candidate.py --out audit.json
- run: steercert check audit.json --min-efficiency deployed_vector=0.5 --min-ranking 0.7

docs.title: Sites, functionals and gradients
docs.text:
An intervention site is a tensor in the forward pass, for example the output of decoder block \(\ell\) at the last token. A behavioural functional \(\phi(x)\) is a scalar computed from the model's output, for example the log-mean-exp logit of a set of toxic tokens minus that of a reference set.

For example \(i\) let \(h_i\) be the activation at the site and \(g_i = \partial \phi_i / \partial h_i\) its gradient. Adding \(\alpha w\) to \(h_i\) changes the behaviour by

\[ \Delta\phi_i(\alpha w) = \alpha\, g_i^\top w + O(\alpha^2). \]

steercert.hf.collect obtains every \(g_i\) in one backward pass per batch, because examples in a causal-LM batch do not interact.

docs.title: The effect Gramian and certificates
docs.text:
Over a set of examples define the mean gradient \(\bar g\) and the effect Gramian

\[ W = \mathbb{E}[g g^\top]. \]

For a unit direction \(w\) the three first-order certificates are

certificate formula predicts signed \(\lvert \bar g^\top w \rvert\) the mean effect of a small step mean absolute \(\mathbb{E}\lvert g^\top w \rvert\) the typical per-example effect RMS \(\sqrt{w^\top W w}\) the root-mean-square per-example effect

The best RMS direction is the leading eigenvector of \(W\), with value \(\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}}\). The best signed direction is \(\bar g / \lVert\bar g\rVert\).

Efficiency divides a certificate by its maximum: \(\text{RMS eff}(w) = \sqrt{w^\top W w / \lambda_{\max}}\) and \(\text{signed eff}(w) = \lvert\cos(w, \bar g)\rvert\). The latter equals the alignment \(\rho\) when \(w\) is a probe.

Always report absolute leverage

Efficiency is a ratio. It can rise while the leverage it is a ratio of collapses, as happens late in depth and late in denoising. The report always prints \(\lVert\bar g\rVert\) and \(\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}}\) next to it.

docs.title: Rank diagnostics
docs.text:
• stable rank \(\operatorname{tr} W / \lambda_{\max}\): near 1, per-example gradients are nearly collinear.
  • participation ratio \((\operatorname{tr} W)^2 / \lVert W\rVert_F^2\).
  • entropy effective rank: \(\exp\) of the entropy of the normalised spectrum.

All of these, and every certificate, are invariant under orthogonal changes of basis of the residual stream (tested in tests/test_geometry.py).

docs.title: Dark directions
docs.text: Given a probe \(p\) (what a monitor reads), the RMS dark direction maximises \(w^\top W w\) subject to \(w \perp p\). It is the strongest way to move the behaviour that the monitor cannot see. subspace_dark_direction does the same for a whole set of monitors. A high dark-direction efficiency with a low probe efficiency is a read/write gap (finding SC201).

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
A candidate should beat construction-matched controls, not just random directions. Three families are provided:

  • isotropic: random unit vectors. In high dimension they are nearly orthogonal to everything, so beating them is a weak test.
  • shuffled-label probe: the same probe recipe fitted on permuted labels.
  • sign-randomised gradient: the mean of per-example gradients with random signs. If the stable rank is near 1 this control collapses onto \(\bar g\) (median cosine near 1). It then cannot discriminate, which raises finding SC102.

docs.title: Step sizes
docs.text: Activation norms grow with model width, so a fixed absolute step is not comparable across models. measure_effects(alpha_mode="residual-median") scales \(\alpha\) by the median activation norm at the site.

docs.title: Second order
docs.text: steercert.hf.directional_derivatives returns exact first and second directional derivatives through Hessian-vector products. With a curvature bound \(M\), the first-order certificate dominates while \(\alpha < 2\lvert\bar g^\top w\rvert / M\) (geometry.usable_radius).

docs.title: Contributing to steercert
docs.text: Thank you for helping. Bug reports, questions, new integrations and documentation fixes are all welcome.

docs.title: Getting help and reporting problems
docs.text:
• Questions and usage help: open a GitHub issue with the question label.
  • Bugs: open an issue using the bug template. Include the steercert version (python -c "import steercert; print(steercert.__version__)"), the model and site, and a minimal script. A saved report (report.to_json(...)) helps.
  • Security-relevant findings (for example a way a monitor can be evaded that should not be public yet): email the maintainer at the address in pyproject.toml instead of opening a public issue.

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/bleymambwe/steercert
cd steercert
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate   # .venv\Scripts\activate on Windows
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pytest
ruff check src tests && ruff format --check src tests && mypy src
mkdocs serve

The Hugging Face tests use tiny random models and need no downloads.

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text:
1. Open an issue first for anything larger than a small fix, so the design can be agreed before you write code.
  2. Add tests. Numerical code needs a check against a closed form, a finite difference, or another library's behaviour, not only a smoke test.
  3. Keep the core (geometry, audit, controls, probes, stats, two_clock) free of non-NumPy dependencies. Framework code goes in hf.py or integrations/ with lazy imports.
  4. A new integration needs a test that skips cleanly when the library is absent, and a section in docs/integrations.md.
  5. A new reporting rule needs a finding code, a test that it fires (and only then), and a row in docs/findings.md.
  6. Update CHANGELOG.md under "Unreleased".

docs.title: Releasing (maintainers)
docs.text:
1. Update src/steercert/_version.py and CHANGELOG.md.
  2. Tag vX.Y.Z and push the tag. The release workflow builds the package and publishes it to PyPI with trusted publishing. Zenodo archives the GitHub release and mints a DOI.

docs.title: Code of conduct
docs.text: Everyone taking part is expected to follow the Code of Conduct.

docs.title: Diffusion language models
docs.text:
In an absorbing-state (masked) diffusion language model every site has two time coordinates: depth and denoising step. Committed tokens are frozen. A probe at step \(t\) therefore reads evidence that is already committed, while a write at step \(t\) can only act through positions that are still masked. Decodability tends to rise along the denoising clock while write leverage falls. Autoregressive generation is the special case that unmasks left to right.

steercert.two_clock provides:

docs.title: The counting baseline and the shape gap
docs.text:
Part of the fall in leverage is simple counting: fewer positions remain writable. counting_baseline(writable_counts) is that content-free curve. shape_gap(curve, baseline) is the largest difference between the measured and baseline curves after peak normalisation. A small gap means the measured decay is explained by counting alone. Schedule-aware steering methods should show a gap before claiming a mechanism.

from steercert.two_clock import counting_baseline, shape_gap

gap = shape_gap(measured_write_norms, counting_baseline(masked_payload_counts))

docs.title: The lattice
docs.text:
from steercert.two_clock import Lattice

lattice = Lattice(read=auc_matrix, write=gbar_norm_matrix, steps=progress, depths=(1, 2, 3, 4))
lattice.write_decreasing()     # F1: leverage never rises along the clock
lattice.clocks_dissociated()   # F2: read and write peak at different steps

Fill each cell by calling steercert.audit on gradients collected at that depth and denoising step.

docs.title: The exact construction
docs.text: make_schedule, analytic_read_auc, analytic_write_norm and remask_recoverable implement a closed-form model in which the population probe and the mean gradient are orthogonal at every step. Remasking committed write positions restores leverage without changing decodability. That one operation underlies remask-based defences and remask-based attacks.

docs.title: Findings and reporting rules
docs.text:
Every report carries a list of findings. info findings state a substantive result. warning findings mark a condition that limits what the audit can support. Use steercert check --fail-on-warnings to block on them in CI.

Code Severity Raised when What to do SC101 warning fewer than 32 examples collect more certificate examples SC102 warning stable rank < 2, or sign-randomised controls align with \(\bar g\) report the stable rank; rely on shuffled-label controls SC103 warning controls built without states/labels (isotropic only) pass states and labels to build shuffled-label probes SC201 info probe RMS efficiency < 0.3 while the dark direction keeps > 0.9 a monitor on this probe misses most ways the behaviour can move SC202 info probe RMS efficiency > 0.7 the probe is also an effective actuator at this site SC203 warning a candidate does not beat the best shuffled-label control treat the candidate as no better than chance construction SC204 info no leverage exists outside the read direction(s) every effect lies inside what the monitor reads SC301 warning certificate ranks measured effects at Spearman < 0.7 do not use the certificate to select directions at this site SC302 warning measurements used absolute step sizes use alpha_mode="residual-median" before comparing models SC303 info reference/gramian_top was not measured include it so measured efficiencies are defined

docs.title: Where the rules come from
docs.text:
These rules came from errors found while auditing real experiments:

  • Reporting relative efficiency alone hid a 16-fold fall in absolute leverage between the embedding and final layer of Pythia-70M.
  • Sign-randomised controls reached a median cosine of 0.99 to the mean gradient in a model whose effect Gramian had stable rank 1.1–1.3. Steering audits have observed the symptom (arXiv:2608.24335); stable rank is the cause.
  • Pooling absolute step sizes across model widths can manufacture apparent scaling trends (arXiv:2608.08159).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
steercert needs Python 3.10 or newer. The core depends only on NumPy.

pip install steercert                     # NumPy core: audits, geometry, controls, two-clock tools
pip install "steercert[hf]"               # + PyTorch and Hugging Face transformers adapter
pip install "steercert[steering-vectors]" # + steering-vectors integration
pip install "steercert[repeng]"           # + repeng integration
pip install "steercert[nnsight]"          # + nnsight / NDIF remote collection
pip install "steercert[all]"              # everything above

The lm-evaluation-harness integration only writes .pt files, so it needs steercert[hf]. Install lm-eval to run the evaluations themselves.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/bleymambwe/steercert
cd steercert
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pytest

docs.title: Check the installation
docs.text:
steercert demo

prints an audit of a synthetic site and needs no model download.

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text: All integrations import their target library lazily. Every one of them uses the block-output convention: layer k means the output of decoder block k, which is steercert.hf.Site.block(k).

docs.title: steering-vectors
docs.text:
from steercert.integrations.steering_vectors import from_steering_vector, to_steering_vector

vectors = from_steering_vector(sv)          # {Site.block(k): np.ndarray}
better = to_steering_vector({k: direction})  # back to a SteeringVector

SteeringVector.apply adds the vector at every selected token. Audit it with collect(..., positions="all"), which sums gradients over positions and is the exact derivative for that edit. tests/test_integrations.py checks that the logits steering-vectors produces equal those of steercert's own edit.

docs.title: repeng
docs.text:
from steercert.integrations.repeng import from_control_vector, to_control_vector

repeng trains on hidden_states[k + 1] and controls the output of block k. These match except at the last block, where Hugging Face applies the final norm first.

docs.title: lm-evaluation-harness
docs.text:
from steercert.integrations.lm_eval import save_steer_config, load_steer_config

save_steer_config("dark.pt", model, {Site.block(6): report.directions["reference/dark_rms"]},
                  coefficient=0.03 * residual_norm)

lm_eval run --model steered --model_args pretrained=EleutherAI/pythia-160m,steer_path=dark.pt --tasks hellaswag

This measures the capability cost of any audited direction on standard benchmarks. load_steer_config reads existing configs, including ones derived from SAE features, so they can be audited. The tests replicate lm-eval's hook resolution and add semantics and check them against steercert's edit.

docs.title: nnsight and NDIF (experimental)
docs.text:
from nnsight import LanguageModel
from steercert.integrations.nnsight import collect_nnsight

model = LanguageModel("meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B")
data = collect_nnsight(model, prompts, layers=[8, 16, 24], functional=phi, remote=True)
report = steercert.audit(data.gradients[Site.block(16)])

With remote=True the trace runs on the National Deep Inference Fabric, which serves open models far larger than a laptop can hold. Locally, on nnsight 0.7, gradients and states match steercert.hf.collect to 1e-6. Remote behaviour depends on NDIF's deployed models and policies. Validate on a small model first.

docs.title: Any other source
docs.text: steercert.audit takes plain arrays. Gradients from TransformerLens hooks, pyvene interventions or a custom JAX model work unchanged, as does any direction such as an SAE decoder row, a classifier head or a CAST condition vector.

docs.title: 1. A synthetic site (no model)
docs.text:
steercert.synthetic.decoupled_site builds activations, labels and gradients where the cosine between the read direction and the dominant write direction is set by hand. It shows the central phenomenon in isolation.

import steercert
from steercert.synthetic import decoupled_site

site = decoupled_site(n=4000, overlap=0.1)
fit, held_out = slice(0, 2000), slice(2000, None)
probe = steercert.fisher_probe(site.states[fit], site.labels[fit])

report = steercert.audit(
    site.gradients[held_out],
    {"probe": probe},
    probe="probe",
    states=site.states[held_out],
    labels=site.labels[held_out],
)
print(report.summary())

The probe reads the label with AUC above 0.95 but captures under 20% of the achievable leverage. reference/dark_rms, the best direction orthogonal to the probe, keeps nearly all of it. The report raises finding SC201.

docs.title: 2. A Hugging Face model
docs.text:
An honest audit uses three disjoint prompt splits:

Split Used for fit fitting the probe (or training the steering vector) certificate per-example gradients for the audit test finite interventions that validate the certificate 
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
import steercert
from steercert.hf import Site, collect, measure_effects, token_ids, token_logit_difference

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("EleutherAI/pythia-70m").eval()
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("EleutherAI/pythia-70m")
for p in model.parameters():
    p.requires_grad_(False)

phi = token_logit_difference(token_ids(tok, ["stupid", "idiot", "pathetic"]),
                             token_ids(tok, ["kind", "great", "lovely"]))
site = Site.block(2)  # output of decoder block 2

probe = steercert.logistic_probe(
    collect(model, tok, fit_prompts, site, gradients=False).states[site], fit_labels
)
cert = collect(model, tok, cert_prompts, site, phi)
report = steercert.audit(cert.gradients[site], {"probe": probe}, probe="probe",
                         states=cert.states[site], labels=cert_labels, site=str(site))

measured = measure_effects(model, tok, test_prompts, site, report.direction_matrix(), phi,
                           alpha=0.03, alpha_mode="residual-median")
report = report.with_measurement(measured)
print(report.summary())
report.to_json("audit.json")

examples/02_toxicity_probe_audit.py is a complete runnable version on RealToxicityPrompts.

docs.title: 3. Reading the report
docs.text:
• RMS eff: share of the best achievable RMS effect, from the certificate.
  • meas eff: the same ratio from finite interventions on held-out prompts.
  • absolute leverage |g_bar|: always read efficiencies next to it. A high efficiency at a site with almost no leverage means little.
  • ranking (Spearman): whether the certificate orders the directions the way measured effects do. Below 0.7, finding SC301 warns against using it to select directions at that site.

See Findings and reporting rules for every finding code.

docs.title: Test suite
docs.text:
pytest runs about 90 tests. Those that need PyTorch use tiny randomly initialised GPT-2, GPT-NeoX and Llama models with a byte-level tokenizer, so CI downloads nothing. They check:

  • Gradients against finite differences at the embedding, block-output and final-norm sites, for last-token and all-token edits, on all three architectures.
  • Batch independence: per-example gradients from batch size 1 equal those from batch size 8.
  • Site mapping: states at every Site equal the corresponding Hugging Face output_hidden_states tensor to 1e-10.
  • Second order: Hessian-vector-product curvature against finite second differences.
  • Integrations: steering-vectors' and lm-evaluation-harness's add hooks produce the same logits as steercert's edit. nnsight collection matches the direct Hugging Face path.
  • Geometry: closed-form cases, optimality of dark directions, and invariance under orthogonal reparameterisation.
  • Reporting rules: each finding fires, and only, under its condition.

docs.title: Reproduction of a research artifact
docs.text:
steercert was extracted from a research codebase that audited toxicity probes in Pythia models. Running one stored cell (Pythia-70M, split seed 17, output of block 2, step 3% of the median residual norm) through the package's public API on CPU reproduces the stored GPU result:

quantity steercert stored abs. diff probe AUC (held-out) 0.8477 0.8477 0 alignment \(\rho\) 0.1064 0.1064 2e-5 absolute leverage \(\lVert\bar g\rVert\) 1.3158 1.3158 1e-5 stable rank 4.3186 4.3191 5e-4 probe certificate RMS efficiency 0.1659 0.1659 1e-5 step size \(\alpha\) 0.3741 0.3741 6e-8 probe measured RMS efficiency 0.1841 0.1840 9e-5 dark direction measured RMS efficiency 0.9941 0.9944 4e-4

The ranking Spearman (0.868 vs 0.824) depends on the random control directions included in the ranked set, which were drawn from a different generator.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• The bundled functionals are next-token proxies, not generated-text measures.
  • The certificate is first order. Check usable_radius or the measured curvature before trusting it at large step sizes.
  • Some architectures (Llama's RMSNorm) compute internally in float32 even in float64 models. This bounds finite-difference agreement at about 1e-4.

docs.title: steercert.audit
docs.text:
The sensor/actuator audit: one call that turns gradients into a report.

:func:audit answers, for every candidate direction at one intervention site:

  • how much of the available write leverage it captures (certificate efficiency),
  • how that compares with the best direction, a probe-orthogonal "dark" direction, and construction-matched controls, and
  • optionally, how well the certificate predicts held-out finite interventions.

The result is an :class:AuditReport that serialises to JSON and can be checked against thresholds in CI with :func:check_report or the steercert check command.

docs.title: Finding dataclass
docs.text:
A reporting-rule result attached to an audit.

severity is "info" for a substantive result worth stating and "warning" for a condition that limits what the audit can support.

docs.title: EffectMeasurement dataclass
docs.text:
Measured finite-intervention effects for named directions.

slopes[name] holds one symmetric finite-difference slope (phi(+alpha) - phi(-alpha)) / (2 alpha) per held-out example.

docs.title: DirectionRow dataclass
docs.text: Certificate and (optional) measured statistics for one direction.

docs.title: AuditReport dataclass
docs.text: Result of :func:audit. Serialise with :meth:to_dict or :meth:to_json.

docs.title: row(name)
docs.text: Return the row for direction name.

docs.title: direction_matrix(include_controls=True)
docs.text: Names and stacked unit directions, ready for finite-intervention measurement.

docs.title: check(**thresholds)
docs.text: Return threshold failures; see :func:check_report for arguments.

docs.title: summary(include_controls=False)
docs.text: Plain-text table for terminals and logs.

docs.title: with_measurement(measured)
docs.text: Return a copy with held-out measured effects attached and ranking computed.

docs.title: audit(gradients, directions=None, *, probe=None, states=None, labels=None, read_basis=None, controls=True, measured=None, site=None, seed=0, metadata=None)
docs.text:
Audit read and write directions at one intervention site.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default gradients ndarray

(n_examples, width) per-example gradients of the behavioural functional at the site. Use a split disjoint from the one used to fit probes and from the one used for measured.

required directions Mapping[str, ndarray] | None

Named candidate directions, for example steering vectors to compare.

None probe str | ndarray | None

The read direction a monitor uses: either the name of an entry in directions or a vector (stored as "probe"). Enables the probe-orthogonal dark directions and read/write-gap findings.

None states ndarray | None

Optional activations and binary labels from a held-out split. Adds an AUC column and enables shuffled-label probe controls.

None labels ndarray | None

Optional activations and binary labels from a held-out split. Adds an AUC column and enables shuffled-label probe controls.

None read_basis ndarray | None

Optional (k, width) rows spanning everything a monitor reads. Adds reference/dark_subspace, the best direction invisible to all of them.

None controls bool | ControlSet

True builds the default families, False disables them, or pass a :class:~steercert.controls.ControlSet.

True measured EffectMeasurement | Mapping[str, ndarray] | None

Held-out finite-intervention slopes (see :func:steercert.hf.measure_effects).

None site str | None

Free-text label of the intervention site, stored in the report.

None

docs.title: check_report(report, *, min_ranking=None, min_efficiency=None, max_efficiency=None, min_mean_gradient_norm=None, min_stable_rank=None, fail_on_warnings=False)
docs.text:
Compare a serialised report with thresholds and list every failure.

Intended for regression tests: for example, require a deployed steering vector to keep at least half of the available leverage after a fine-tune. min_efficiency and max_efficiency map direction names to bounds on certificate RMS efficiency.

docs.title: steercert.geometry
docs.text:
Write-side geometry: the effect Gramian and certificates built from it.

Every function here operates on NumPy arrays and needs no deep-learning framework. Model instrumentation lives in :mod:steercert.hf.

Notation

gradients has shape (n_examples, width). Row i is the derivative of a scalar behavioural functional phi_i with respect to the activation at one intervention site. directions has shape (n_directions, width); rows are normalised internally, so only their orientation matters.

The effect Gramian is W = E[g g^T]. It is never formed as a dense width x width matrix: all spectral quantities come from a thin SVD of the gradient matrix.

docs.title: EffectGeometry dataclass
docs.text:
Spectral summary of the effect Gramian W = E[g g^T].

Attributes:

Name Type Description trace float

tr(W), the mean squared gradient norm.

leading_eigenvalue float

lambda_max(W); sqrt of it is the RMS effect of the best direction.

stable_rank float

tr(W) / lambda_max(W). Near 1, per-example gradients are nearly collinear and sign-randomised controls become degenerate.

participation_ratio float

tr(W)^2 / ||W||_F^2.

entropy_effective_rank float

exp of the Shannon entropy of the normalised spectrum.

entropy_rank_over_width float

Effective rank divided by the activation width.

mean_gradient_norm float

||g_bar||, the absolute signed write leverage. Report it next to every relative efficiency.

top_eigenvalues tuple[float, ...]

Leading eigenvalues of W.

top_direction ndarray

Leading eigenvector of W, the RMS-optimal write direction.

docs.title: to_dict()
docs.text: JSON-serialisable summary (the direction is omitted).

docs.title: unit(vector, eps=EPS)
docs.text:
Return a unit-norm copy of vector.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the vector is zero or not finite, because its direction is undefined.

docs.title: cosine_abs(left, right, eps=EPS)
docs.text: Absolute cosine between two vectors, or 0.0 if either is null.

docs.title: project_orthogonal(vector, normal)
docs.text: Project vector onto the orthogonal complement of normal.

docs.title: mean_gradient(gradients)
docs.text: Mean behavioural gradient g_bar; its norm is the absolute write leverage.

docs.title: rho(gradients, probe)
docs.text:
Alignment |cos(probe, g_bar)| between a read direction and the mean gradient.

rho = 1 means the probe points exactly where a signed write is most effective; rho = 0 means writing along the probe has no first-order mean effect.

docs.title: effect_geometry(gradients, top_k=10)
docs.text:
Compute the effect-Gramian spectrum and rank diagnostics.

The leading direction is the first right singular vector of the gradient matrix, oriented so that it has a non-negative inner product with the mean gradient.

docs.title: certificate_scores(gradients, directions)
docs.text:
First-order write certificates for each candidate direction.

Returns:

Type Description signed, mean_absolute, rms:

|E[g^T w]|, E[|g^T w|] and sqrt(E[(g^T w)^2]) for every unit-normalised row w of directions. The signed score predicts the mean effect of a small step; the other two keep per-example effects that cancel in the mean.

docs.title: signed_dark_direction(gradients, probe)
docs.text:
Best signed-effect direction constrained to be orthogonal to probe.

This is (I - p p^T) g_bar normalised: a direction the probe cannot see that still moves the behaviour on average.

docs.title: rms_dark_direction(gradients, probe)
docs.text:
Best RMS-effect direction constrained to be orthogonal to probe.

Solves the Rayleigh problem for P W P with P = I - p p^T through the SVD of the projected gradients.

docs.title: usable_radius(gradients, direction, curvature)
docs.text:
Step size up to which the first-order certificate is trustworthy.

For a unit direction with signed certificate s and a bound M on the directional second derivative, the linear term dominates the quadratic remainder while alpha < 2 s / M.

docs.title: second_order_prediction(alpha, first_directional, second_directional)
docs.text: Second-order Taylor prediction alpha * d1 + alpha^2 / 2 * d2 per example.

docs.title: stacked_mean_gradient_direction(gradient_blocks)
docs.text:
Optimal unit-energy direction for writing at several sites at once.

Each block has shape (n_examples, width_at_site) and rows must refer to the same examples. The result concatenates the per-site mean gradients and normalises them under one total-energy constraint.

docs.title: steercert.hf
docs.text:
Hugging Face transformers adapter.

Collects activations and per-example behavioural gradients at an intervention site, and measures finite interventions at the same site. Both use the same hook, so the gradient and the edit always refer to the same tensor.

Gradients are taken through an additive zero tensor inserted at the site (h -> h + delta with delta = 0 requiring grad). This works with frozen weights, half precision, and any architecture whose decoder blocks can be located. Per-example gradients come from one backward pass per batch because examples in a causal LM batch do not interact.

Requires torch and transformers (pip install steercert[hf]).

docs.title: Site dataclass
docs.text:
Where in the network a direction is read or written.

Site.block(k) is the output of decoder block k. This is the convention used by steering-vectors, repeng and lm-eval-harness. Site.embeddings() is the input to block 0. Site.final_norm() is the output of the final normalisation, which Hugging Face returns as the last element of hidden_states.

docs.title: from_hidden_state_index(index, n_blocks) classmethod
docs.text:
Map an index into Hugging Face output_hidden_states to a site.

0 is the embeddings, 1..n_blocks-1 are block outputs, and n_blocks is the final-norm output. Negative indices count back.

docs.title: parse(text) classmethod
docs.text: Parse "embeddings", "final_norm", "block.3" or "block:3".

docs.title: Collected dataclass
docs.text:
Activations, gradients and functional values gathered by :func:collect.

With positions="last" each row is the last real token. With positions="all" states are mean-pooled over real tokens and gradients are summed over them, which is the exact derivative for a vector added at every position (as steering-vectors and lm-eval-harness do).

docs.text:
Dotted name of the module whose output is site, relative to root.

root defaults to model. The embeddings site is the input of block 0 and has no module whose output it is, so it raises ValueError.

A smooth next-token proxy for behaviours such as toxicity or sentiment. It is not a generation-level measure; validate any conclusion on generated text.

One forward and one backward pass per batch cover every site at once.

docs.title: measure_effects(model, tokenizer, prompts, site, directions, functional, *, alpha=0.03, alpha_mode='residual-median', positions='last', batch_size=16, max_length=128)
docs.text:
Measure symmetric finite-difference effects of each direction.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default directions Mapping[str, ndarray] | tuple[list[str], ndarray]

Mapping of names to vectors, or report.direction_matrix().

required alpha float

Step size. With alpha_mode="residual-median" (default) it is a fraction of the median activation norm at the site, which keeps steps comparable across models of different width. "absolute" uses it as-is.

0.03 positions str

"last" edits the last real token; "all" edits every real token.

'last' Notes

Use prompts disjoint from those used to fit probes and compute the certificate, so the ranking check in :func:steercert.audit is held out.

docs.title: directional_derivatives(model, tokenizer, prompts, site, directions, functional, *, batch_size=8, max_length=128)
docs.text:
Exact first and second directional derivatives at the last token.

Uses Hessian-vector products; no dense Hessian is formed. The second-order term bounds the step size over which the first-order certificate is trustworthy (see :func:steercert.geometry.usable_radius).

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text:
Converters between steercert and other interpretability and steering libraries.

Each submodule imports its target library lazily, so import steercert never requires them. Install the extras you need, for example pip install steercert[steering-vectors].

Layer convention: every library here indexes by decoder block output, which is :meth:steercert.hf.Site.block.

Interoperate with steering-vectors <https://github.com/steering-vectors/steering-vectors>_.

SteeringVector.layer_activations maps a decoder-block index to a vector that is added to that block's output at every selected token, so audit it with positions="all" unless you restrict token_indices to the last token.

Interoperate with repeng <https://github.com/vgel/repeng>_ control vectors.

ControlVector.directions maps a layer id to a vector that ControlModel adds to the output of decoder block layer_id at every position. repeng reads its training activations from hidden_states[layer_id + 1], which is the same tensor except for the last block, where Hugging Face applies the final norm first.

Export to and import from lm-evaluation-harness steering configs.

lm-eval-harness evaluates a steered model with::

lm_eval run --model steered \
    --model_args pretrained=EleutherAI/pythia-160m,steer_path=steer.pt \
    --tasks hellaswag

steer.pt maps a hookpoint (a module name relative to model.base_model) to a dict with steering_vector, steering_coefficient, action, bias and head_index. With action="add" the vector is added to that module's output at every position, so the matching certificate uses positions="all".

Typical use: pick directions with :func:steercert.audit (for example a dark direction or the Gramian-top direction), export them here, and measure their capability cost on standard benchmarks.

Collect certificate gradients through nnsight <https://nnsight.net>_.

With remote=True the same code runs on the National Deep Inference Fabric (NDIF), which serves open models up to hundreds of billions of parameters. That makes certificates on 8B-405B models possible without a local GPU.

Status: experimental. Verified locally with nnsight 0.7 on small models, where gradients and states match :func:steercert.hf.collect to 1e-6; remote execution depends on NDIF's deployed models and its policy for gradients and custom code, which can change. Validate a remote result against a local run on a small model first.

Example

from nnsight import LanguageModel # TransformersModel on nnsight >= 0.8 from steercert.hf import token_ids, token_logit_difference from steercert.integrations.nnsight import collect_nnsight model = LanguageModel("meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B") phi = token_logit_difference(token_ids(model.tokenizer, ["hate"]), token_ids(model.tokenizer, ["love"])) data = collect_nnsight(model, prompts, layers=[8, 16, 24], functional=phi, remote=True)

model is an nnsight.LanguageModel (TransformersModel on nnsight >= 0.8) or any nnsight.NNsight wrapper with a tokenizer. Results are keyed by :meth:steercert.hf.Site.block and feed straight into :func:steercert.audit.

docs.title: Probes, controls, statistics
docs.text:
Read-side directions: linear probes fitted on activations.

All probes return a unit direction in the original activation coordinates, so they can be audited with :func:steercert.audit exactly like a steering vector. They depend only on NumPy; use any external probe (scikit-learn, a trained classifier head) by passing its weight vector instead.

Control directions for steering experiments.

A steering result is only as informative as the comparator it beats. Three families are provided, matching current practice (SteerCheck, arXiv:2608.24335):

isotropic Uniform random unit directions. In high dimensions they concentrate near orthogonality to everything, so beating them is a weak test. shuffled_label_probe The same probe recipe fitted on permuted labels. Matches the construction while breaking the label link. sign_randomized_gradient The mean of per-example gradients with random signs. Matches the gradient construction while destroying its shared sign. When the effect Gramian has stable rank near 1, per-example gradients are nearly collinear and this control collapses back onto the mean gradient, so it must be reported with the stable rank (see :func:sign_control_is_degenerate).

Small statistics helpers with no SciPy dependency.

Synthetic sites where read quality and write alignment are set independently.

Used by the examples, the tests and steercert demo. The construction shows that a probe can read a label perfectly while pointing almost orthogonally to the direction that moves behaviour, and lets each quantity be checked against its known population value.

docs.text: Class-mean difference mu_1 - mu_0, the ActAdd / CAA steering vector.

docs.title: fisher_probe(states, labels, shrinkage=0.001)
docs.text:
Shrinkage linear discriminant (Sigma + gamma I)^{-1} (mu_1 - mu_0).

shrinkage is relative to the mean eigenvalue of the pooled within-class covariance, so it is invariant to the overall activation scale.

docs.text:

Full-batch gradient descent; deterministic. The weight vector is mapped back to raw activation coordinates before normalisation.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default separation float

3.0 overlap float

0.1 gradient_rank int

docs.title: steercert.two_clock
docs.text:
Two-clock analysis for diffusion (and autoregressive) language models.

In an absorbing-state (masked) diffusion LM every intervention site has two time coordinates: depth l and denoising step t. A committed token is frozen, so a probe at step t reads evidence that has already been committed, while a write at step t can only act through positions that are still masked. Read information therefore tends to rise along the denoising clock while write leverage falls. Autoregressive generation is the special case where positions are unmasked left to right.

This module provides:

  • :class:Lattice, a container for read and write measurements on the (depth, step) grid with the falsifier checks F1 and F2;
  • :func:shape_gap and :func:counting_baseline, which test whether a controllability curve carries attribute-specific structure or is explained by the shrinking set of writable positions alone (falsifier F5);
  • the exact closed-form construction (:func:make_schedule, :func:analytic_read_auc, :func:analytic_write_norm) in which the read and write directions are orthogonal at every step.

docs.title: Lattice dataclass
docs.text:
Read and write measurements on a (depth, denoising step) grid.

Attributes:

Name Type Description read ndarray

(n_depths, n_steps) decodability, for example probe AUC.

write ndarray

(n_depths, n_steps) absolute write leverage, for example |g_bar|.

steps ndarray

Denoising progress for each column, increasing (0 = fully masked).

depths tuple

Labels for each row.

docs.title: write_decreasing(tolerance=0.0)
docs.text: F1 check per depth: write leverage never rises along the denoising clock.

docs.title: clocks_dissociated()
docs.text: F2 check per depth: decodability and leverage peak at different steps.

docs.title: joint_optimum(read_weight=0.5)
docs.text: Step that maximises a weighted geometric mean of normalised read and write.

docs.title: Schedule dataclass
docs.text: An absorbing-diffusion unmasking order over read and write positions.

docs.title: normalise_curve(values)
docs.text: Divide a non-negative curve by its maximum (zero curves are returned unchanged).

docs.title: shape_gap(curve, baseline)
docs.text:
Largest difference between two curves after each is peak-normalised.

A small gap means the measured controllability curve has the same shape as the content-free baseline, so its decay is explained by counting alone.

docs.title: counting_baseline(writable_counts)
docs.text:
Content-free write-leverage curve from the number of writable positions.

If each still-masked payload position contributes an equal, independent gradient component, the mean-gradient norm scales as the square root of the number of writable positions. Schedule-aware steering methods should beat this curve, which costs one count per step and no training.

docs.title: make_schedule(n_read, n_write, seed=0, order='random')
docs.text: Build a schedule; order='identity' is the autoregressive case.

docs.title: analytic_read_auc(schedule, step, kappa, sigma)
docs.text:
Population AUC of the optimal linear readout of committed evidence.

With m committed read positions the pooled statistic has separation d' = kappa sqrt(m) / sigma and AUC = Phi(sqrt(2) d').

docs.title: analytic_write_norm(schedule, step, gamma)
docs.text: Mean-gradient norm at step; proportional to sqrt(masked write positions).

docs.title: remask_recoverable(schedule, step, n_remask)
docs.text:
Write positions made writable again by remasking n_remask recent write commits.

Read commitments are untouched, so remasking raises controllability at unchanged decodability. The same operation underlies remask-based safety defences and remask-based attacks.
